summary_html: The child is **removed from the home** and placed in foster care under court order or emergency authority. Federal statutes tie funding to safety findings, judicial oversight, and permanency planning.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — removal, reasonable-efforts, and permanency requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of placement decisions

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Reversing an order of temporary custody, the court held that Connecticut's summary removal scheme is constitutional only because it confines coercive intervention to serious physical illness, serious physical injury or immediate physical danger and requires that measures short of removal be used where possible.
key_cases.relevance: Foster placement is permissible only after the narrowly drawn statutory criteria and the less restrictive alternatives analysis described here are satisfied.
key_cases.quote: This phrase requires that various steps short of removal from the home be used when possible in preference to disturbing the integrity of the family.

key_cases.holding: The court construed the commitment-revocation statute to be triggered only by application of the persons or agencies it specifies, so others could not invoke the Juvenile Court's power to revoke a commitment.
key_cases.relevance: Once a child is committed to the commissioner and placed, only the enumerated parties can move the court to end that placement.
key_cases.quote: Under § 17-62 (f), one of those specified persons or agencies must apply to trigger the Juvenile Court's power to revoke the commitment to the welfare commissioner.

key_cases.holding: The court held that juvenile court jurisdiction over a youth committed to the department does not necessarily end at eighteen, but found neither § 17a-11 nor § 46b-129 supplied a basis for jurisdiction to order services on these facts, and remanded with direction to dismiss.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the durational limits of a commitment to the commissioner and the placement obligations that flow from it.
key_cases.quote: although the jurisdiction of the Superior Court for Juvenile Matters does not necessarily cease when a youth committed to the department turns eighteen

key_cases.holding: The court reversed the Appellate Court, holding that § 46b-129(j)(4) carries a presumption in favor of in-state placement and remanding because the record did not show the trial court applied the correct good cause standard to the out-of-state placement motion.
key_cases.relevance: It sets the good cause showing the commissioner must make before a committed child may be placed outside Connecticut.
key_cases.quote: Upon review of the record, we cannot be confident that the trial court applied the correct legal standard to adjudicate the petitioner's motion for out-of-state placement.

key_cases.holding: The court held that § 46b-129 (p), which gives foster parents a right to be heard and comment, does not prohibit a trial court from permitting foster parents to intervene in neglect proceedings, rejecting the contrary rule of In re Ryan C., and reversed.
key_cases.relevance: It is the current Connecticut authority on the party status of foster parents in the proceedings that determine whether a child stays in their placement.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the statute does not prohibit a trial court from permitting foster parents to intervene in such proceedings.

common_failures: Failure to consider less restrictive alternatives

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Issuance of the ex parte order of temporary custody or order to appear

notice_requirements.timing: At the commencement of any proceeding on behalf of a neglected, uncared-for or abused child or youth, and again at the preliminary hearing on an order of temporary custody or order to appear
content_required: The parent or guardian has the right to counsel and must be so informed by the judge
If the parent or guardian is unable to afford counsel, counsel will be provided
The parent or guardian has the rights of confrontation and cross-examination

The court may also appoint counsel for the parent or guardian without a request if it determines the interests of justice so require (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-136(a)); in a proceeding in which the custody of a child is at issue the judge must provide an attorney for the child

Cost of appointed counsel in the civil juvenile session is shared as agreed by the Division of Public Defender Services and the Judicial Department, and the court may order a party found able to pay to reimburse that cost (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-136(b)(1))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 46b-135 or 46b-136

statutory_basis.citation_text: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-135(b) (right to counsel and cross-examination); see also § 46b-136 (appointment of attorney; payment) and § 46b-129(c)(1) (advisement at the preliminary hearing)

notice_requirements.timing: In any involuntary Superior Court proceeding for foster care placement of, or termination of parental rights to, an Indian child, once the court knows or has reason to know an Indian child is involved
content_required: Notice of the right of intervention

If the parent, Indian custodian or tribe cannot be identified or located, like notice to the Bureau of Indian Affairs Regional Director or Secretary (federally recognized tribe) or to the Commissioner of Children and Families (tribe recognized by the state of Connecticut), who then has 15 days to give the required notice
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: The Indian child, parent, Indian custodian or tribe may petition to invalidate a foster care placement or termination of parental rights action that violated state or federal law (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-116n)

statutory_basis.citation_text: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-116d (required notice to Indian parent, Indian custodian and Indian tribe of state foster care and termination of parental rights proceedings), Connecticut Indian Child Welfare Act

parent_rights_at_moment: Right to know where child is going
what_to_say: Do you have a court order for removal?
What is the specific imminent danger?
Where are you taking my child?
what_not_to_do: Do not physically interfere with lawful removal
